overview.description: Hindersche (meaning 'Backwards') is a rare and traditional reverse trick-taking game played exclusively in the central Black Forest of Germany. It is an Ace-Ten game where the objective is to *avoid* taking tricks containing card points. It is noted for its antiquity, using a 36-card pack and being played anticlockwise.

history.origins: A local game from the Kinzig and Wolf valleys. It is believed to be over 200 years old, traditionally played by farmers and foresters.
timeline: 1933: First written mention of the game.
2014: Official rules codified and published online for tournament play.
Present: Annual 'World Championships' held in Schapbach, Germany.
history.evolution: Developed as a 'negative' counterpart to a game called 'Viersche' (Forwards). It has preserved antique features like anticlockwise play and the Ten ranking low.
history.cultural: A point of regional pride and a rare survivor of localized card game cultures.

setup.deck: 36-card German-suited pack (A, K, O, U, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6). Ranking: A > K > O > U > 9 > 8 > 7 > 6 > 10 (Note the low Ten!).
setup.dealing: Play and dealing are ANTICLOCKWISE. Dealing varies but usually involves batches of cards to reach 9 cards per player.

rules.objective: Avoid taking tricks with high point values. The player with the MOST points in a round loses a point (mark on the slate).
rules.gameplay:
1. The player to the right of the dealer leads.
2. You must follow suit if possible.
3. **Trumps**: The last card dealt to the dealer determines the trump suit.
4. **The Reverse Rule**: If you cannot follow suit, you MUST play a trump if you have one.
keyRules: Follow the legal action constraints defined for Hindersche.
Round outcome is resolved by the scoring method: Ace-Ten scoring (A=11, 10=10, K=4, O/Q=3, U/J=2).
Winning condition: Avoid taking tricks with high point values.

strategy.basic: Void suits early to smear high-value cards (Ace and Ten) onto opponents.
strategy.intermediate: Manage your trumps carefully. If you have low trumps, use them to win 'cheap' tricks so you don't have to take expensive ones later.
strategy.advanced: The 'March': If you have extremely high cards, you might try to win every single trick, which can sometimes result in a special bonus or clearing multiple strokes.
tips: Leading a Ten is called 'selling a Tenner' - hope that someone else is forced to buy it!
Save a low card in each suit to exit tricks when needed.

phases.label: Deal
phases.notes: Anticlockwise dealing. Deal 9 cards to each player. Last card to dealer determines trump.

phases.label: Trick Play
phases.notes: Anticlockwise play. Follow suit if able. Trump if can't follow. Highest suit/trump wins anticlockwise.

phases.label: Round End
phases.notes: Count points. Highest scorer gets stroke. Continue until 4 strokes marked.

play_card.description: Play one card to the trick. Follow suit if able; if unable to follow suit you may play any card (including trump). Highest trump wins; if no trump, highest card of the led suit wins. Trick winner leads to the next trick.
play_card.constraints: Must follow suit if holding a card of the led suit; otherwise may play any card. Legal when it is your turn in trick play.

trumpConfig.trumpSuitRanking: Trump Jack (Old Man) highest, next Jack (same colour) second, then A-K-Q-10-9-8-7-6.
trumpConfig.overtakingRule: Must follow suit if able; if unable may play any card including trump.

trickConfig.leadRestrictions: Forehand (right of dealer) leads first trick.

edgeCases.text: Schleipfen: a player may take a trick they did not win if no one objects before the next lead.
Tie for most points: tied players hold a playoff deal to determine who receives the mark.
March (100+ points or all 9 tricks): in Phase 1 all three opponents get one mark; in Butzen march erases 2 marks and opponents each add 1.

customActions.description: System counts trick points (A=11, 10=10, K=4, O=3, U=2); player with most points receives one stroke; game continues until one player has 4 strokes.
customActions.constraints: Automatic after last trick of the round.

engine.handRankingSystem: Ace-Ten point scoring for tricks: A=11, 10=10, K=4, Q=3, J=2; trump Jacks 12 each. Highest total in tricks loses the deal.
engine.deckDescription: A 36-card German deck (Skat pack) made by removing the 2s through 5s from a standard 52-card pack, leaving Ace, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack, Queen, and King in each of the four suits. Used for Hindersche and other German trick-taking games where the aim is to avoid taking point cards.
engine.suitDescription: The four German suits (Acorns, Leaves, Hearts, Bells) each contain nine ranks in the 36-card pack. Suit order and symbolism follow the traditional German deck used across central Europe for games like Skat and Hindersche.
engine.rankDescription: Ranks in each suit are Ace (often high), King, Queen, Jack, 10, 9, 8, 7, and 6. Point values for scoring are typically assigned to certain ranks (e.g. Jacks, Aces) in Hindersche, where the goal is to avoid taking tricks containing these cards.

synthesis.shortDescription: A rare German reverse trick-taking game where the goal is to take as few points as possible, played anticlockwise with a 36-card German deck.
